...[believ]ed, not studied. And I act thus as if I were providing a defense for eloquence against its detractors, which is greater than my purpose. For we are writing not about this, but about the elegance of the Latin language, from which, nevertheless, a step is made toward eloquence itself. But if anyone is not eloquent, he should only then not be rebuked if he was unable to emerge as such, not if he fled from this labor. He, however, who knows not how to speak elegantly and commits his thoughts to writing, especially in theology, is most impudent; and if he says he does this deliberately, he is most insane—though there is no one who would not wish to speak elegantly and fluently; but since this does not fall to their lot, they wish (perverse as they are) to seem unwilling, or certainly that they ought not to speak so. And therefore they say that the pagans spoke in this manner, and that it is not fitting for Christians to speak in the same way—as if those whom I have named spoke in the manner of these men, and not in the manner of Cicero and the rest of the pagans, whose manner of speaking they have neither recognized nor experienced. Not the language of the pagans, not grammar, not rhetoric, not dialectic, and the other arts are to be condemned (since the apostles wrote in the Greek language), but the dogmas, the religions, and the false opinions concerning the practice of virtues, through which we climb into heaven.

The other sciences and arts, however, lie in a middle ground, which you may use both well and badly. Wherefore, I beseech you, let us strive to arrive there, or at least very near, where those luminaries of our religion arrived. You see with how wondrous an ornament the garments of Aaron were distinguished, how the Ark of the Covenant, how the Temple of Solomon: by this, eloquence seems to me to be signified, which (as the noble tragic poet says) is the queen of things and perfect wisdom. <margin>Euripides in Hecuba.</margin> And so, others adorn private houses—these are those who study civil law, canon law, medicine, philosophy, contributing nothing to divine matters; let us adorn the house of God, so that those entering it may be moved to religion not by the mold of neglect to contempt, but by the majesty of the place. I cannot restrain myself from saying what I feel. Those ancient theologians seem to me like certain bees flying even into distant pastures...

# Thousand-Gold-Hammer
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in Jiangnan, two to three feet tall. Treats poison from snake or insect bites; apply to sores to grow muscle and stop pain.</gloss>

# Tu-Luo-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in Lingnan mountain valleys. Leaves are fine and long. Sweet, warm, non-toxic. Treats cold abdominal qi, pain, and abdominal masses. Can also be pounded into juice and taken warm.</gloss>

# Yi-Dai-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in the mountain valleys of Guizhou like An-mountain. Leaves are round, two to three feet high. Harvest in the second month. Sweet taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats blood-qi fatigue and lower back and knee weakness. Treats wind-related looseness, emaciation, lack of color, and weak yang. No seeds. Women with old blood-stasis soak it in wine to drink. It expels disease extremely quickly, hence the name Yi-Dai [Wait-and-See].</gloss>

# Yaowang-Cao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Bitter, green with juice. Sweet taste, neutral, non-toxic. Resolves all poisons, stops nosebleeds and vomiting blood, and relieves restlessness.</gloss>

# Jinzi-Root
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows on Siming Mountain. More than a foot tall. Leaves are round, thick, and lustrous; they do not wither in winter. Root as thick as a finger. Also called Genzi. Bitter taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats knotted masses in the chest and abdomen, long-term stagnation, and pain beneath the navel. Also treats ghost-qi, shooting pain, cholera, gu-poison, and sudden bloody stools. Grind and take with wine.</gloss>

# Lu-Yao
<gloss>Cangqi says: Grows in the Hu states. Resembles thatch, yellow-red color. Salty taste, warm, non-toxic. Treats internal damage and blood stasis, stops pain, cures the five internal organs, removes evil-qi, and supplements deficiency. For postpartum blood conditions, boil in water and take. Also pound and apply to injured areas. Shizhen says: The "Waitai Mi" secret method for treating internal horse-kick injuries: take one liang of Lu-yao powder, mix with a cup of cow's milk and take.</gloss>

<column-break/>

# Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao-Cao <gloss>Windless-Shaking-Grass</gloss>
<gloss>Shiyi says: Grows in the Da-Qin [Roman] Empire and Lingnan. Harvest on the fifth day of the fifth month in the various mountain wilds. It is often found there. The head is like a pellet; the tail is like a bird's tail. Two leaves open and close; it moves by itself. It is said that its name is Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao-Cao, but the object is different. Duan Chengshi’s "Yang Za Yan" says Yazhou produces a Dancing Grass; it has three leaves, like Jue-ming; one leaf is at the tip of the stem, two leaves reside halfway up the stem opposite each other. When people approach it, sing, or clap hands, it shakes like dancing. According to this, it is the Tang "Beauty Grass," and is of the same type as the Wu-Feng-Yao-Yao. Also according to the "Classic of Mountains and Seas": On Mount Guyao, the Emperor’s daughter died, and her horse transformed into a plant; its leaves overlap, flowers are yellow like rabbit silk (dodder); wearing it makes others love you. Guo Pu’s annotation says it is also called "Wild-Husband Grass." This statement is similar to Chen Cangqi’s remark about wearing it to encourage love. It is one and the same.</gloss>

<gloss>Tao says: Grows in the mountain valleys of Guangnan. Has pods about two feet long, with thin leaves like paper, the size of cicada wings. Treats evil spirits in small boys and girls. Put it in a red silk bag and wear it on the arm to ward off evil. This grass grows in the South, hence the name. It is different from the Yi-Nan of the Daylily.</gloss>

kauft, sondern kauft mit seinem Schatten. Das Wertzeichen
wirkt daher nur, soweit es innerhalb des Prozesses den Preis
der einen Ware gegenüber der anderen oder jedem Warenbesitzer
gegenüber Gold vorstellt. Ein bestimmtes relativ wertloses
Ding, Stück Leder, Papierzettel u. s. w., wird zunächst gewohn-
heitsmäßig Zeichen des Geldmaterials, behauptet sich jedoch nur
als solches, indem sein Dasein als Symbol durch den allgemeinen
Willen der Warenbesitzer garantiert wird, d. h. indem es gesetz-
lich konventionelles Dasein und daher Zwangskurs erhält. Staats-
papiergeld mit Zwangskurs ist die vollendete Form des Wert-
zeichens, und die einzige Form des Papiergelds, die unmittelbar
aus der metallischen Zirkulation oder der einfachen Waren-
zirkulation selbst herauswächst. Kreditgeld gehört einer höheren
Sphäre des gesellschaftlichen Produktionsprozesses an und wird
durch ganz andere Gesetze geregelt. Symbolisches Papiergeld
ist in der Tat durchaus nicht verschieden von der subsidiären
Metallmünze, nur in weiterer Zirkulationssphäre wirkend. Wenn
die bloß technische Entwicklung des Maßstabs der Preise oder
des Münzpreises und weiter die äußerliche Umformung des Roh-
goldes in Goldmünze schon die Einmischung des Staats hervor-
riefen und damit die innere Zirkulation von der allgemeinen
Warenzirkulation sich sichtbar schied, so wird diese Scheidung
vollendet durch die Entwicklung der Münze zum Wertzeichen.

It therefore seems as if the value-sign directly represents the value of commodities, in that it presents itself not as a sign of gold, but as a sign of the exchange value that is merely expressed in the price but exists solely within the commodity. This appearance is, however, false. The value-sign is directly only a price-sign, hence a gold-sign, and only via a detour a sign of the commodity’s value. Gold has not sold its shadow like <term>Peter Schlemihl</term> <note>a literary character who loses his shadow</note>, but rather buys with its shadow. The value-sign therefore functions only insofar as it represents the price of one commodity against another or, to every commodity owner, against gold within the process. A certain relatively valueless thing, a piece of leather, a slip of paper, etc., first becomes a sign of the money-material by habit, yet only maintains itself as such in that its existence as a symbol is guaranteed by the general will of the commodity owners, i.e., in that it receives a legally conventional existence and therefore forced currency <term>Zwangskurs</term> <gloss>legal tender status</gloss>. State paper money with forced currency is the completed form of the value-sign, and the only form of paper money that grows directly out of metallic circulation or simple commodity circulation itself. Credit money belongs to a higher sphere of the social production process and is regulated by entirely different laws. Symbolic paper money is indeed not at all different from subsidiary metal coinage, only acting in a wider sphere of circulation. If the purely technical development of the standard of prices or the mint price, and further the external transformation of raw gold into gold coins, already summoned the interference of the state, and thereby the internal circulation visibly separated itself from general commodity circulation, then this separation is completed by the development of the coin into a value-sign.

**The second** had a dream of seven fat and as many lean years, which Joseph interpreted for him. Because of this, he placed Joseph over the entire land of Egypt and treated all his relatives, the children of Israel, with kindness, Genesis 37, 39, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 50.

**The third** oppressed the children of Israel severely and commanded that all their newborn sons be killed, Exodus 1, 2.

**The fourth** would not let the children of Israel depart from Egypt according to the Lord's command. Instead, he hardened his heart even after he saw God's wonders. He hurried after the children of Israel as they departed from his land and was drowned in the Reed Sea <note>original: "SchilffMeer," commonly known as the Red Sea</note> along with all his people, Exodus 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15; 2 Kings 17; Psalms 134, 135; Romans 9. Eusebius calls this man Cenchrem in his *Chronicles* <note>original: "in Chronicis"</note>.

**The fifth** captured the city of Gezer. He married his daughter to King Solomon and gave her Gezer as a wedding gift, 1 Kings 3, 7, 9, 11.

**The sixth** was otherwise named Shishak. He supported Solomon's adversaries, Jeroboam and Hadad, 1 Kings 11. He marched against Rehoboam, Solomon's son, captured the city of Jerusalem, and plundered the Temple along with the royal palace, 1 Kings 14.

**The seventh** was called Pharaoh Necho. He slew the pious King Josiah and captured Josiah's son, Jehoahaz, 2 Kings 23; 2 Chronicles 35. He was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylon, Jeremiah 46.

**The eighth** was named Pharaoh Hophra. Jeremiah prophesied against him when he was led into Egypt by the remaining people of Israel during the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah 43, 44.

<column-break/>

**Phariseus, Pharisei,** <note>original Greek: "φαρισαῖος, φαρισάδης," translated as Pharisee</note>

**Pharisees** are "Separated Ones," distinct people, masters of the law, interpreters of the law, scribes, interpreters of scripture, and masters of scripture. This was the name given to the strictest sectarians among the Jews, Acts 26. They separated themselves from other common people and wanted to be regarded as teachers of the law. They interpreted the scripture according to the letter and according to the bare history, as Origen writes in his commentary *On Matthew* <note>original: "super Matthæum"</note>.

They sat themselves in Moses' seat, Matthew 23. They claimed the keys of the kingdom of heaven for themselves, Luke 11. They mixed the scripture with philosophy and held that the Messiah would begin a physical, earthly kingdom. They also wanted to declare what fortune or misfortune a person would have based on the hour of their birth, as Epiphanius writes in *Against Heresies* <note>original: "contra Hærefes"</note>.

They also said that whatever happened to a person, good or evil, was an unavoidable decree of God. Yet they allowed that man had a free will in some cases, according to Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>original: "Antiq. Iud."</note>, Book 13, Chapter 19, and Book 2. <note>Josephus was a first-century Jewish historian who described the different Jewish sects.</note>

They established many human laws so that they might nullify the commandments of God, Matthew 15, 23; Mark 7; Luke 11; Acts 15.

They honored the LORD with their lips, and with their mouths they drew near to him, but their heart was far from him, Matthew 15.

They placed heavy, unbearable burdens on the necks of men, but they would not move them with a single finger, Matthew 23.

They did all their works so that they would be seen by the people. They made their phylacteries <note>original: "Denckzettel," small leather boxes containing scripture worn during prayer</note> broad and the tassels on their clothes large. They loved to sit at the head of the table and in the synagogues, and they enjoyed being called "Rabbi" by men, Matthew 23; Luke 11.

We shall not detain the reader here with the barred *Y* of the Mayas. It is simply a spelling abbreviation for the preposition *yetel*, "by, with." This sign could be compared to the barred *K* of Lower Breton, which stands for the particle *Ker*, "at the home of, near." <note>Lower Breton is the Breton spoken in western Brittany.</note>

As for the half-vowel OU, in Quiché it is rendered by *v* or *u* before another vowel; for example in *vatch*, "face," pronounced *ouatch*. However, if the letter *u* is preceded by a *Q*, it has no more sound of its own than it would have, for example, in the Spanish *Quebrado* or the French *quérir*. Thus one will pronounce *quel*, "flat stone," and *quem*, "cloth, to weave," as if they were written *gkel* or *kkel*, *gkem* or *kkem*. Sometimes the following E is marked with a diaeresis, to show that the sound of this letter does not merge with that of the preceding one, or perhaps that it is open. Such is the case, for example, with *quëh*, "deer," pronounced *gkeh* or better *ghèc'h* (in Maya *Ceh*). Let us add that most often this silent *u* after Q is left out, for example in *qax*, "sorrow"; *qel*, "parakeet"; *qil*, "brother"; *qop*, "to cut," etc., etc.

In Maya, U sometimes has a value like that of English W in *William*, *well*, when it is followed by another vowel; for example in *uah*, "to nail," and *uinic*, "man," pronounced *wac'h*, *winik*. But most often, even in this case, it has an <term>interflatile</term> <gloss>breathed or glided</gloss> sound, which we shall deal with when discussing the consonants. We have already seen that sometimes, even when followed by another vowel, it remains a vowel itself.

V does not exist in Maya, at least in Beltrán and the authors who followed him. As will be seen shortly, it is replaced by B. The use of V in Tzeltal seems much the same as in Quiché. The memory says that a bronze cow stood at this passage, having been set up by the Chalcedonians; for both this and those were the monument of the beautiful heifer. And this bull was called Thracian from the Thracian living around the place. Just as it was once called by the same name as this greater one. Dionysius <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer</note> says about this that its narrowest part ferries that whole thing, and those who have become sea-faring through the wave-swept [strait]; these are the prodigies who reveal such a Byzantine strait, and the historians use "heifer." But this geographer is accustomed to calling the Byzantine strait the "Thracian cow." And the prodigies call the Hellespont strait [the cow] over all the parents before the Thracian one came to be, and the geographer likewise records those on the stages in the strait, interpreting it. It must be noted that this, and all the local differences, the Thracian cow is what pours out toward the Pontus; the northern part is its own, the southern is that of the Propontis. And they know that the mouth of the Pontus will appear more accurately as the Hellespont of the Chalcedonians; for it is very close to the beginning of Dionysius, the waves and by Cyzicus, just as he himself says, and others not toward the whole place. But his scope of the Hellespont and that passage toward the Pontus is the remainder; therefore, let us also go to the widths themselves. Its northern [part] and the northern one toward the Pontus, that which is after the Hellespont; and after the Pontus, that which is toward the north is the mouth of the Pontus. These things have ambiguities because the ancients called the parts by Abydos the Hellespont, and the Pontus the Hellespont; others also [called] the whole Pontus. And the northern one is that toward the mouth of the Pontus; regarding this, those around Heracles despaired of the Hellespont. Others [call] the Aegean source of the Hellespont toward the north, as perhaps Homer does; the ocean toward the widths and the Hellespont. And I seem to follow Dionysius in these things, as it is necessary to divide [them] and [as] water of an exit; so that the Hellespont is the narrow channel, and the Pontus. And both are from the honor toward the Pontus, the one being the Thracian Bosphorus itself. And the one called personal, the Bosphorus is said to be the fugitive toward the Pontus itself, and the parts toward the shore the Hellespont; the chasm is greater, with the shore sources. And [it is] because Dionysius has also traveled well through both straits.

There will be many bodhisattvas of great power there, turning the wheel of no turning back <note>The irreversible Dharma wheel: teaching that leads beings to a stage from which they never fall back from the path to awakening.</note>, of sharp faculties in the teaching of that Victor. By them the Buddha-field will be made beautiful. His Hearers will be many, beyond number; their measure can never be grasped. They will have the six higher knowledges <note>Supernormal powers such as the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, memory of former lives, miraculous abilities, and knowledge that the defilements are exhausted.</note> and the three knowledges, and great miraculous power; they will abide firmly in the eight liberations <note>A series of eight meditative attainments leading to freedom from attachment.</note>.

When he expounds this supreme awakening, his power of miracles will be beyond conception. Gods and humans as many as the sands of the Ganges will always join their palms toward him. He will remain for twelve intermediate aeons. The true Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate aeons. Likewise the semblance <note>The later period when the outward forms of the teaching survive.</note> of that Best of Two-Legged Ones <note>An epithet of a Buddha, supreme among humans.</note> will remain for twenty intermediate aeons.

Then once again the Blessed One addressed the whole assembly of monks: "Monks, have faith in this; understand it. This Hearer of mine, the Elder Mahākātyāyana, will honor, revere, respect, make offerings to, esteem and venerate eight thousand koṭis of Buddhas <note>A koṭi is an Indian counting unit, usually taken as ten million.</note>. And after those Thus-Gone Ones have passed fully into nirvana, with the seven kinds of precious substances, namely gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald <note>original: "rdo'i snying po", literally "heart of stone", rendering Sanskrit aśmagarbha.</note>, and seven kinds of precious

His life span will be twelve intermediate aeons. His true Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate aeons. The semblance of the true Dharma will also remain for twenty intermediate aeons.

Then at that time the Blessed One spoke these verses:

With words that will never prove otherwise, today, all you monks, listen to me. This Hearer of mine, the Elder Kātyāyana, will make offerings to the Guides <note>The Buddhas, who lead beings out of suffering.</note>. After the Guides of the world have passed fully into nirvana, he will build many kinds of stupas for them. He will show them honor in many ways, and will also make offerings with incense and flowers.

Having attained his final body, he will become a Victor in a completely pure field. Having brought this very wisdom to perfection, he will teach thousands of koṭis of living beings. Honored by the world together with its gods, he will become the Light-Maker, the Chief, the Blessed One. His name will be Light of Jambū River Gold <note>Sanskrit Jāmbūnadaprabhāsa.</note>. He will also fully carry across koṭis of gods and humans.

Bodhisattvas, and likewise many Hearers, will be in that Buddha-field, beyond measure and beyond number. Having completely abandoned all arising and perishing <note>That is, freed from the cycle of becoming and ceasing.</note>, they will make the Buddha's teaching beautiful.
